item.title: The Ingredient You Won't Find on the Label
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial chemical used since the 1950s to make hard plastics and line metal cans, and it acts as an endocrine disruptor that mimics estrogen in the body
  • A 2016 University of Missouri study found that dogs eating canned food for just two weeks saw circulating BPA levels roughly triple, even when one of the diets was labeled BPA-free
  • Exposure has been linked to fertility issues, diabetes, obesity, neurological changes, thyroid disruption including hyperthyroidism, gut microbiome imbalance, and altered serum chemistry
  • BPA is not only in cans — it also shows up in kibble bag linings, plastic food and water bowls, storage bins, measuring cups, and any hard plastic your dog chews on regularly
  • Practical fixes include switching to fresh food, using stainless steel or ceramic bowls, transferring kibble to glass containers, filtering drinking water, and choosing brands with transparent packaging testing

You read the label and choose the good brand. You look for real meat first — no by-products or mystery fillers. Yet still, because of how modern pet food is packaged, stored, and shipped, a chemical your dog is being exposed to twice a day never appears on any ingredient list.

Independent research keeps confirming that pet foods packaged in metal cans and plastic bags carry measurable amounts of an industrial chemical called BPA — one that ends up in your dog's bloodstream within days of switching diets. And even brands marketed as "BPA-free" do not always live up to the label.

What Is BPA (and Why Is It Getting So Much Attention)?

Bisphenol A is a synthetic chemical that has been used since the 1950s to make hard plastics and to line the inside of metal food and beverage cans. You will find it in water bottles, food storage containers, cash-register receipts, canned goods, plastic bowls, and a long list of everyday items. The chemistry that makes BPA useful — it hardens plastic, prevents corrosion, and creates a smooth barrier between food and metal — also means small amounts leach out of packaging and into the food or drink stored inside.

What makes BPA a bigger deal than most industrial chemicals is that it is an endocrine disruptor. That means it mimics the hormone estrogen and can interfere with the body's own hormone signaling. In humans and animals, this has been linked to a range of concerns from reproductive issues to metabolic disease. Despite decades of controversy, the FDA still approves BPA as a "food contact material" for most applications.1,2,3

How BPA Ends Up in Your Pet’s Food Bowl

The main exposure route for pets — as for humans — is diet. A 2017 industry analysis found that 81% of dog food cans tested contained BPA, and 95% of cat food cans contained PVC (a related plastic chemical). Every single can tested had one or the other, or both.4

Canned pet food is the obvious source, but kibble is not off the hook. The plastic bags used to package dry food can also contain BPA, and the chemical can migrate into the food during storage — especially with heat, moisture, or extended shelf life. In one study, researchers who tested dogs before switching them to canned food found that baseline BPA was already detectable in the animals' blood, even though the dogs had been eating kibble (more on this study later).

That is a strong hint that dry food packaging is a real exposure source, not just cans. Every step in the supply chain — from ingredient sourcing to final packaging to storage on your kitchen shelf — is a potential contact point.5

Beyond food packaging, BPA also shows up in plastic pet water bowls, food bowls, measuring cups, food storage bins, toys, and any hard plastic your dog chews on or drinks from all day. Warm dishwasher cycles and prolonged sun exposure can accelerate the leaching of BPA from these products, meaning a bowl that was low-exposure when new can become a bigger source of contamination over time as it ages, scratches, and cycles through repeated heat.

What the Research Actually Shows

The most cited study on BPA in dogs came out of the aforementioned 2016 study, published in the Science of the Total Environment journal. A research team from the University of Missouri took blood and stool samples from 14 healthy privately owned dogs before switching them to one of two commercially available canned diets, one of which was marketed as BPA-free. After just two weeks on either diet, the dogs' circulating BPA concentrations had roughly tripled, jumping from an average of 0.7 nanograms per milliliter at baseline to 2.2 nanograms per milliliter.6

The elevated BPA did not just circulate quietly. It correlated with changes in the dogs' plasma bicarbonate levels — a marker of shifting metabolism — and with meaningful alterations in the gut microbiome. Specifically, elevated BPA appeared to reduce populations of a specific bacterium that helps metabolize BPA and related environmental chemicals. In other words: more BPA in, less ability to clear it out.7,8

Dr. Cheryl Rosenfeld, a professor of biomedical sciences in the University of Missouri College of Veterinary Medicine and one of the study authors, made a point worth repeating: Dogs share our homes, our food supplies, and our environmental exposures. What shows up in their blood is often a preview of what is showing up in ours. In her words, our canine companions may be the best bio-sentinels for human health concerns.9

What BPA May Do Over Time

Chronic BPA exposure in pets has been associated with a growing list of health concerns. Even short-term consumption — as brief as two weeks — has been shown to affect metabolic markers and the microbiome. Longer-term exposure has been tied to:

  • Fertility and reproductive issues
  • Increased risk of diabetes and insulin resistance
  • Obesity
  • Neurological changes
  • Thyroid disruption — including links to hyperthyroidism in cats and thyroid dysfunction in dogs
  • Gut microbiome imbalance
  • Alterations to serum chemistry and metabolism

As with most environmental toxins, the concern is not a single meal. It is the cumulative effect of daily low-dose exposure over the 10 to 15 years a pet is with you.

Small numbers compound. And because BPA acts on hormone-driven systems like thyroid, reproductive, and metabolic system, the effects often do not show up as a dramatic event but as a slow drift toward chronic conditions that get chalked up to "just aging." Integrative and holistic veterinarians increasingly view this kind of background chemical load as one piece of the puzzle behind the rise in chronic disease across companion animals.10,11

Even ‘BPA-Free’ Is Not Always What It Sounds Like

Here is a wrinkle worth knowing about: One of the two canned diets in the featured study was labeled BPA-free, yet still produced a rise in circulating BPA in the dogs eating it. Both diets showed BPA in the actual food.12,13 There are a couple of reasons this happens:

  • Testing standards vary — A can may be labeled BPA-free based on its can lining alone, while the food inside was already contaminated during processing or from ingredient supply chains.
  • Many BPA-free products simply substitute a closely related compound like BPS or BPF — These behave similarly in the body and are less well studied. Emerging research on these bisphenol substitutes suggests they may carry many of the same endocrine-disrupting properties as BPA itself, and in some cases may be more persistent in the environment. "BPA-free" is a start, but it is not automatic safety.

The takeaway is not to distrust every label. It is to remember that packaging chemistry is complex, regulation lags behind the science, and no single certification tells the whole story. Combining multiple strategies — better packaging, better storage, and better bowls — makes more difference than chasing any one label.

What You Can Actually Do

You cannot eliminate BPA exposure for your pet any more than you can for yourself. But you can meaningfully reduce it, and small choices repeated daily are what actually shift a pet's total chemical burden over time. Practical steps that add up:

  • Move away from canned food when possible. Fresh, gently cooked, or frozen pet foods packaged in cartons, glass, or Tetra Pak avoid the can lining problem entirely.
  • If you feed kibble, consider transferring the food to an airtight glass or stainless steel storage container. Do not leave it sitting in the plastic bag for weeks. Be aware, though, that transferring the kibble out of the original bag, where it is most likely packed in nitrogen to displace oxygen and prevent spoilage, can lead to the food going rancid much more quickly. Transfer to an alternate storage container only if you are keeping small amounts of food on hand and purchasing more frequently.
  • Choose brands that use BPA-free packaging and are transparent about it. Some brands publish their testing; those are worth rewarding.
  • Ditch plastic bowls. Switch to stainless steel or ceramic for both food and water. Plastic bowls are also known for causing chin acne in some pets.
  • Do not microwave plastic containers. Heat accelerates leaching. Same goes for putting hot food in plastic.
  • Wash bowls daily with hot soapy water. Biofilm builds up faster on plastic and can trap contaminants.
  • Filter your pet's drinking water. A quality filter reduces overall chemical load, especially if you are on municipal water.
  • Skip plastic toys that your dog chews for hours. Choose rubber, cotton, or natural materials for heavy chewers.

From an integrative and holistic veterinary perspective, the goal is not a chemical-free life — it is not achievable in the modern world. The goal is to reduce cumulative load enough that your pet's natural detoxification pathways can keep up. Support that with clean water, quality diet, and thoughtful choices about packaging and containers, and you have done most of what is realistic.13

A Wider Lens on Pet Food

BPA is not unique; it is part of a larger conversation about industrial chemicals that are quietly present in your pet's food, water, and environment, like heavy metals, PFAS "forever chemicals," phthalates, and other endocrine disruptors that never appear on any ingredient panel because they are not ingredients in the technical sense. They are packaging residues, processing byproducts, and environmental contaminants that end up in the final product without ever being disclosed to the consumer.

Independent research groups have been raising red flags on this for years. And dogs — with their shorter lifespans, faster metabolisms, and total dependence on whatever we put in their bowl — often show the effects of these exposures years before humans in the same household do.

Chronic diseases that veterinarians have watched steadily climb in dogs and cats over the past few decades, such as cancer, autoimmune conditions, thyroid disorders, allergies, obesity, diabetes, all have plausible ties to the cumulative chemical burden of modern life. That is what makes companion animals such useful early-warning systems, and it is also what makes it worth paying attention.14

Your dog cannot read the label. They also cannot ask why their food comes in a can lined with an estrogen-mimicking chemical, or why their water bowl leaches plastic residues after a hot summer day. You are the one who does that work for them.

Small changes — a switch from canned food or kibble to fresh food, from plastic bowls to stainless steel, from plastic chew toys to natural products — add up over a lifetime in a way that matters more than most pet parents realize. Talk to an integrative or holistic veterinarian if you want to build a more comprehensive plan around reducing your pet's environmental toxin load, especially if they are already dealing with thyroid, gut, or metabolic issues where BPA and similar chemicals are known to play a role.

The best ingredient in any dog's dinner is the one you thought carefully about. And sometimes the most important part of that thought is not what is on the label — it is what is not. What is not disclosed. What is not tested. What is not regulated. Being the person who thinks about that on your pet's behalf is one of the quiet, ongoing ways of loving them well.

Sources and References

  • 1,10,13 Just Food for Dogs, November 27, 2023
  • 2 U.S. FDA, April 20, 2023
  • 3 NIH, Bisphenol A
  • 4 Ecology Center, June 27, 2017
  • 5,6,8,12 Science of The Total Environment, 1 February 2017, Volume 579, Pages: 1804-1814
  • 7,9,11,14 Science Daily, December 19, 2016

item.title: Germ Warning: Lab Tests Reveal Stunning Levels on These Pet Items
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Dog toys are loaded with bacteria, so it’s important for the health of everyone in the household that toys are washed at least monthly; also dispose of any toys that are old, broken, chewed up or weathered
  • Select toys that are a good size for your dog and have no small or sharp parts
  • Certain dog toys should only be played with under your close supervision, for example, toys with batteries
  • There are “toys” that should be avoided entirely, including strings and rocks, and plastic toys containing toxins such as BPA
  • Keep in mind that interactive play with your dog will always be more fun and stimulating for him than a basketful of toys

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 22, 2018.

A television station in Grand Rapids, Michigan featured a segment on bacteria on dog toys. The station worked with a laboratory to analyze the gunk on toys belonging to one of the news reporters' dogs, a Toy Poodle named Henry. They tested exclusively soft toys, and the bacteria counts were so high they had to dilute the samples just to analyze them.

It will come as no surprise to all you dog parents out there that there were hundreds of thousands of bacteria on each toy, as well as on Henry's dog bed. The lab found no E. coli, but did detect thousands of bacterial colonies after calculating the total microbial count from the diluted samples. The same lab also does forensic dust analysis, and has concluded that 60% of the dust in households with pets comes from furry family members.

Needless to say, it's important to wash your dog's toys regularly, especially if she tends to hang on to special soft toys rather than destroying them like many pups do. It's also important to wash plastic dog toys routinely, and dog beds as well.

Chances are the massive amounts of bacteria on her belongings won't bother your pet in the least, but there's a possibility a human family member could become ill after handling a dog toy if they don't wash their hands thoroughly before touching their face, putting food in their mouth, etc.

Washing your dog's toys regularly (once a month is a reasonable guideline) also gives you the opportunity to check their condition and toss the ones that are breaking down or falling apart.

Not Every Dog Toy Is Right for Every Dog

Most dogs in the U.S. have lots of toys, and many pet parents use trial-and-error to determine what type their dog prefers — and which are safest — from a mind-blowing selection of tugs, balls, Frisbees or other types of discs, chew toys, puzzle toys, squeaky toys, stuffed toys and more. And since many pet stores welcome dogs, some pet parents even bring four-legged family members along and allow them to sniff out their favorites.

It's important to select your dog's toys carefully, however, because not every dog toy is a good choice. For example some dogs, especially large breeds, tend to rip soft toys apart within seconds to taste-test the stuffing. There are also dogs that swallow small soft toys whole. So obviously, these types of toys aren't a good choice for certain pets.

Your pup's temperament, size and age all play a role in determining which toys are safe, and there are considerations, too, based on the toy itself (materials used, size, shape and more). It’s recommended to use the guidelines below, compiled by VetStreet,1 to ensure the toys you choose for your dog keep him not only happily playing, but also safe.

Tips for Selecting Safe Dog Toys

  • Choose toys that are the right size for your dog. Giving a small toy to a large dog poses a risk of inhalation and choking. Small balls are especially dangerous, as they can easily become lodged in your dog's trachea.
  • Generally speaking, you should choose large toys for large dogs and smaller toys only for smaller dogs.
  • Avoid toys that have small parts that can be chewed or pulled off.
  • Avoid toys with sharp edges or that can be chewed into sharp points.
  • Be careful letting your dog play with sticks. Avoid sticks that have sharp ends and choose one that is either too long or too short for your dog to jab into the ground when carried vertically (like a straw), as this could cause serious injury to his mouth and/or throat.
  • When playing fetch, avoid toys that are heavy or hard enough to damage your dog's teeth or injure him.
  • If your dog likes to de-stuff toys, be sure he's not eating the stuffing. Some dogs really enjoy stuffing-free toys.

Toys Requiring Close Supervision

  • Supervise your dog when she's playing with long rope-like or tug toys, as they can become wrapped around her neck.
  • If your dog likes to play "rip out the squeaky," offer such toys only when you can safely monitor her play.
  • Be careful with toys that require batteries. If your dog manages to get them out of the toy and swallows them, it can result in battery toxicosis.
  • Be careful with tennis balls. They can be a choking hazard for large dogs, and the abrasive fuzz may wear down teeth if your dog is an aggressive or persistent chewer (normal play will not pose a risk to your dog's teeth).
  • Be careful with toys, such as Frisbees, that may cause your dog to jump up and twist simultaneously. Such movements may lead to leg and back injuries.

'Toys' That Should Be Avoided

  • Dogs shouldn't play with strings, ribbons, pantyhose, socks or rubber bands. These objects may be swallowed and can cause life-threatening complications once in the digestive tract.
  • Don't offer your pet children's toys (such as stuffed animals); they're not designed to withstand the type of play dogs engage in.
  • Avoid any toys stuffed with beads or beans.
  • Don't let your dog play with rocks.
  • Don't give your dog containers (including bags) large enough for him to put his head in. If his head becomes stuck, he'll be unable to get free and may suffocate.
  • If your dog has neck or back problems, such as herniated disks, tug toys should be avoided.
  • Rubber toys with a hole in only one end may form a vacuum that catches your dog's tongue. Either avoid these toys or poke a hole in the other end so a vacuum cannot form.
  • Rawhide chews aren’t recommended for a number of reasons, one of which is because they pose a high risk of choking and intestinal obstruction.

Toys That May Be Toxic

Pet toys are not regulated, so they can be made with virtually any material. Plastic toys, in particular, can be dangerous, as many contain endocrine-disrupting chemicals such as phthalates and bisphenol-A (BPA). Old or weathered toys (such as those left outside) leach higher concentrations of harmful chemicals.

While BPA-free toys are available, the BPA may be replaced with similarly (or more) toxic chemicals, including bisphenol-S (BPS), so this, unfortunately, isn't a reliable indicator of toy safety. Other toxins sometimes found in dog toys include heavy metals (lead, etc.) and formaldehyde.

When looking for new toys, choose those made in the U.S. out of 100% natural rubber, organic cotton, or other eco-friendly and contaminant-free materials. The sniff test is recommended, as toys should have no smell. If a toy you’re considering buying smells strongly of chemicals, put it back.

Testing shows that some tennis balls made for pets contain more contaminants than those made for sports.2 The best toys for pets are usually handmade, by individuals or very small companies and found at local farmer’s markets or sold regionally in small, independent pet stores. Unfortunately, there isn’t a plethora of companies that produce 100% organic toys. However, there are some great all-natural toys you can find online if you go searching.

Types of Toys Dogs Seem to Prefer

Researchers have discovered that regardless of the type of toy, once a dog is completely familiar with the sight, sound, smell and feel of it, boredom sets in. In addition, you may want to avoid those "indestructible" toys your dog can't make a dent in, because research also suggests that dogs enjoy toys they can pull apart and destroy or those that are edible, probably because they view toys the way wolves view their prey.3 They want something they can tear apart and eat.

Of course, offering your dog easily destroyed toys isn't ideal either, as he may accidentally (or intentionally) ingest some of the non-edible pieces. A good alternative is recreational bones (large, raw chunks of beef and bison femur bones), which are extremely enjoyable for most dogs, even though they're not technically "toys."

Treat-release puzzle toys, toys meant to be chewed, and those that make noise or are edible (like a nontoxic dental bone) can also be good options, while toys that are hard, unyielding and silent will probably not be a big hit with your dog.

Finally, don't underestimate your ability to stimulate your dog's interests. A session of playtime with you — playing fetch, tug-of-war or hide-and-seek — will be far more stimulating to your pup than any toy could be. If you need some ideas for playtime, check out these games and activities you can do with your dog.

Sources and References

  • Fox17 West Michigan April 16, 2018
  • 1 VetStreet, July 30, 2014
  • 2 Bark, August 2010
  • 3 Animal Cognition, November 2012, Vol 15, Issue 6, pp 1143-1150

  • Certain dog toys should only be played with under your close supervision, for example, toys with batteries
  • There are “toys” that should be avoided entirely, including strings and rocks, and plastic toys containing toxins such as BPA
  • Keep in mind that interactive play with your dog will always be more fun and stimulating for him than a basketful of toys

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 22, 2018.

A television station in Grand Rapids, Michigan featured a segment on bacteria on dog toys. The station worked with a laboratory to analyze the gunk on toys belonging to one of the news reporters' dogs, a Toy Poodle named Henry. They tested exclusively soft toys, and the bacteria counts were so high they had to dilute the samples just to analyze them.

It will come as no surprise to all you dog parents out there that there were hundreds of thousands of bacteria on each toy, as well as on Henry's dog bed. The lab found no E. coli, but did detect thousands of bacterial colonies after calculating the total microbial count from the diluted samples. The same lab also does forensic dust analysis, and has concluded that 60% of the dust in households with pets comes from furry family members.

Needless to say, it's important to wash your dog's toys regularly, especially if she tends to hang on to special soft toys rather than destroying them like many pups do. It's also important to wash plastic dog toys routinely, and dog beds as well.

Chances are the massive amounts of bacteria on her belongings won't bother your pet in the least, but there's a possibility a human family member could become ill after handling a dog toy if they don't wash their hands thoroughly before touching their face, putting food in their mouth, etc.

Washing your dog's toys regularly (once a month is a reasonable guideline) also gives you the opportunity to check their condition and toss the ones that are breaking down or falling apart.

Not Every Dog Toy Is Right for Every Dog

Most dogs in the U.S. have lots of toys, and many pet parents use trial-and-error to determine what type their dog prefers — and which are safest — from a mind-blowing selection of tugs, balls, Frisbees or other types of discs, chew toys, puzzle toys, squeaky toys, stuffed toys and more. And since many pet stores welcome dogs, some pet parents even bring four-legged family members along and allow them to sniff out their favorites.

It's important to select your dog's toys carefully, however, because not every dog toy is a good choice. For example some dogs, especially large breeds, tend to rip soft toys apart within seconds to taste-test the stuffing. There are also dogs that swallow small soft toys whole. So obviously, these types of toys aren't a good choice for certain pets.

Your pup's temperament, size and age all play a role in determining which toys are safe, and there are considerations, too, based on the toy itself (materials used, size, shape and more). It’s recommended to use the guidelines below, compiled by VetStreet,1 to ensure the toys you choose for your dog keep him not only happily playing, but also safe.

Tips for Selecting Safe Dog Toys

  • Choose toys that are the right size for your dog. Giving a small toy to a large dog poses a risk of inhalation and choking. Small balls are especially dangerous, as they can easily become lodged in your dog's trachea.
  • Generally speaking, you should choose large toys for large dogs and smaller toys only for smaller dogs.
  • Avoid toys that have small parts that can be chewed or pulled off.
  • Avoid toys with sharp edges or that can be chewed into sharp points.
  • Be careful letting your dog play with sticks. Avoid sticks that have sharp ends and choose one that is either too long or too short for your dog to jab into the ground when carried vertically (like a straw), as this could cause serious injury to his mouth and/or throat.
  • When playing fetch, avoid toys that are heavy or hard enough to damage your dog's teeth or injure him.
  • If your dog likes to de-stuff toys, be sure he's not eating the stuffing. Some dogs really enjoy stuffing-free toys.

Toys Requiring Close Supervision

  • Supervise your dog when she's playing with long rope-like or tug toys, as they can become wrapped around her neck.
  • If your dog likes to play "rip out the squeaky," offer such toys only when you can safely monitor her play.
  • Be careful with toys that require batteries. If your dog manages to get them out of the toy and swallows them, it can result in battery toxicosis.
  • Be careful with tennis balls. They can be a choking hazard for large dogs, and the abrasive fuzz may wear down teeth if your dog is an aggressive or persistent chewer (normal play will not pose a risk to your dog's teeth).
  • Be careful with toys, such as Frisbees, that may cause your dog to jump up and twist simultaneously. Such movements may lead to leg and back injuries.

'Toys' That Should Be Avoided

  • Dogs shouldn't play with strings, ribbons, pantyhose, socks or rubber bands. These objects may be swallowed and can cause life-threatening complications once in the digestive tract.
  • Don't offer your pet children's toys (such as stuffed animals); they're not designed to withstand the type of play dogs engage in.
  • Avoid any toys stuffed with beads or beans.
  • Don't let your dog play with rocks.
  • Don't give your dog containers (including bags) large enough for him to put his head in. If his head becomes stuck, he'll be unable to get free and may suffocate.
  • If your dog has neck or back problems, such as herniated disks, tug toys should be avoided.
  • Rubber toys with a hole in only one end may form a vacuum that catches your dog's tongue. Either avoid these toys or poke a hole in the other end so a vacuum cannot form.
  • Rawhide chews aren’t recommended for a number of reasons, one of which is because they pose a high risk of choking and intestinal obstruction.

Toys That May Be Toxic

Pet toys are not regulated, so they can be made with virtually any material. Plastic toys, in particular, can be dangerous, as many contain endocrine-disrupting chemicals such as phthalates and bisphenol-A (BPA). Old or weathered toys (such as those left outside) leach higher concentrations of harmful chemicals.

While BPA-free toys are available, the BPA may be replaced with similarly (or more) toxic chemicals, including bisphenol-S (BPS), so this, unfortunately, isn't a reliable indicator of toy safety. Other toxins sometimes found in dog toys include heavy metals (lead, etc.) and formaldehyde.

When looking for new toys, choose those made in the U.S. out of 100% natural rubber, organic cotton, or other eco-friendly and contaminant-free materials. The sniff test is recommended, as toys should have no smell. If a toy you’re considering buying smells strongly of chemicals, put it back.

Testing shows that some tennis balls made for pets contain more contaminants than those made for sports.2 The best toys for pets are usually handmade, by individuals or very small companies and found at local farmer’s markets or sold regionally in small, independent pet stores. Unfortunately, there isn’t a plethora of companies that produce 100% organic toys. However, there are some great all-natural toys you can find online if you go searching.

Types of Toys Dogs Seem to Prefer

Researchers have discovered that regardless of the type of toy, once a dog is completely familiar with the sight, sound, smell and feel of it, boredom sets in. In addition, you may want to avoid those "indestructible" toys your dog can't make a dent in, because research also suggests that dogs enjoy toys they can pull apart and destroy or those that are edible, probably because they view toys the way wolves view their prey.3 They want something they can tear apart and eat.

Of course, offering your dog easily destroyed toys isn't ideal either, as he may accidentally (or intentionally) ingest some of the non-edible pieces. A good alternative is recreational bones (large, raw chunks of beef and bison femur bones), which are extremely enjoyable for most dogs, even though they're not technically "toys."

Treat-release puzzle toys, toys meant to be chewed, and those that make noise or are edible (like a nontoxic dental bone) can also be good options, while toys that are hard, unyielding and silent will probably not be a big hit with your dog.

Finally, don't underestimate your ability to stimulate your dog's interests. A session of playtime with you — playing fetch, tug-of-war or hide-and-seek — will be far more stimulating to your pup than any toy could be. If you need some ideas for playtime, check out these games and activities you can do with your dog.

  • 2 Bark, August 2010
  • 3 Animal Cognition, November 2012, Vol 15, Issue 6, pp 1143-1150

item.title: Red Means Go but Green Means No for This Snack
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Ripe tomatoes can be given as fresh, healthy pet treats or added to your pet's nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet
  • Tomato's claim to fame is its lycopene content, a carotenoid with "antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antihypertensive, antiplatelet, anti-apoptotic, and protective endothelial effects"
  • A 20-gram serving of fresh tomato contains 24.6 micrograms of lutein and zeaxanthin, which have been greatly valued for their benefits on macular health. Lutein may also have immune health benefits — a 2000 study found that dietary lutein "stimulated both cell-mediated and humoral immune responses in the domestic canine"
  • The green parts of the tomato plant, particularly the stems and leaves, contain a glycoalkaloid called solanine, which is toxic to dogs, cats, and horses, so make sure to keep your pets away from any tomato plants growing in your garden
  • Slice the tomatoes in pieces big enough for your pets to easily swallow. Fresh, raw ripe tomatoes are the best — avoid canned varieties

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 2, 2018.

Tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) bring a distinct sweet-sour taste to any dish and leave a wide array of nutrients at your disposal. But while tomatoes are a ubiquitous part of the human diet, you might find yourself wondering whether this fruit (botanically speaking) can be part of your pet's diet as well. Keep reading to find out how to feed tomatoes to your pets.

Yes, Ripe Tomatoes Are Safe for Your Pets!

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of over-consumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

In the case of tomatoes, the myth is you shouldn't feed tomatoes to pets because they're toxic. The truth is they're safe and good for your pets, as long as you make sure to use only the actual fruit, and in moderation. Tomatoes make great healthy treats or can be added to a nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet. However, the tomato plant — the green stems and leaves — are not safe for your pets. We'll discuss this more in detail later.

Did You Know?

Tomatoes are related to potatoes and chili peppers. They belong to the nightshade plant family, or Solanaceae, along with eggplants and tobacco.1

Tomatoes Are Rich in Vitamin C and Other Antioxidants

The primary reason why tomatoes are so valued in human health is the presence of antioxidant molecules in them. Carotenoids and phenol compounds such as flavonoids are present in this food.2

Another antioxidant that's found in tomatoes is vitamin C, with a 20-gram slice (1/4-inch thick) containing 2.74 milligrams of this nutrient.3 This valuable antioxidant has been associated with disease prevention and free radical-scavenging, and it also helps protect the immune system and fight infections.4 While your dogs and cats can produce their own vitamin C through their liver,5 giving them this nutrient by feeding them a species-appropriate diet would be a boon for their health.

Lycopene — Tomato's Superstar Carotenoid

However, tomato's "claim to fame" is its lycopene content. A single slice of fresh tomato contains 514 micrograms of lycopene,6 which is a carotenoid that gives the red or pink colors to tomatoes as well as grapefruit, watermelon, papaya, and other foods.7

"In humans, lycopene is known to provide numerous benefits, such as supporting heart health."

It has "antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antihypertensive, antiplatelet, anti-apoptotic, and protective endothelial effects" as well.8 A 2010 animal study looked into the anticarcinogenic effects of lycopene in animals. Published in the American Journal of Veterinary Research, the researchers aimed to look at how lycopene affected the growth and apoptosis of osteosarcoma cells in dogs. They found:9

"[L]ycopene may be beneficial during treatment of osteosarcomas. Lycopene did not negatively or positively affect survival of osteosarcoma cells during doxorubicin treatment and independently induced apoptosis in the HMPOS cell line. These findings warrant further in vitro and in vivo studies into the use of this natural compound as an adjuvant antiproliferative, proapoptotic treatment in dogs with osteosarcoma."

Lutein and Zeaxanthin May Help Support Eye Health

A 20-gram serving of fresh tomato contains 24.6 micrograms of lutein and zeaxanthin,10 nutrients that have been greatly valued for their benefits on macular health. Like humans, dogs are also prone to retinal and lens functional decline as they age,11 so providing them with foods that may help supply this nutrient may help maintain their eye health.

Lutein in particular may also have immune health benefits. A 2000 study found that dietary lutein "stimulated both cell-mediated and humoral immune responses in the domestic canine."12

Tomato Fun Fact

Is tomato a fruit or a vegetable? Botanically speaking, it's a fruit, since fruits are defined as "a ripened flower ovary that contains seeds." But because tomatoes are generally used in savory dishes, and not in desserts as most fruits are, it's not uncommon for this crop to be classified as a vegetable. Plus, it's closely related to other fruit-vegetables like eggplants and peppers.13


Whatever you call it, there's no denying that the humble tomato is good for you — and your pet, too!

Note — Keep Your Pet Away from Tomato Plants

So if tomatoes can be good for your pet, why are many people cautioning against them? The reason is that the plant (not the fruit) contains a glycoalkaloid called solanine, which is toxic to dogs, cats, and horses, as noted by the ASPCA. When ingested, it can lead to severe gastrointestinal upset, weakness, hypersalivation, and slow heart rate.14,15

However, keep in mind that solanine is only found in the green parts of the plant: the leaves, stems, flowers, and young green tomatoes. Ripe red tomatoes contain only minute traces of solanine, making them safe for your furry friends.16 So feel free to feed your pets moderate quantities of fresh ripe tomatoes — but make sure to keep them away from the tomato plants growing in your garden.

Where Do Tomatoes Grow?

It's believed that tomatoes were first grown in what's known today as Peru. Today, the top three tomato-producing countries are China, India, and Turkey.17 In the U.S., California and Florida are the top tomato-growing states.18

Choose Organic, 'Spray-Free' Tomatoes

When feeding tomatoes to your pets, make sure to exercise common sense and slice the tomatoes in pieces big enough for your pets to easily swallow. Fresh, raw ripe tomatoes are the best — avoid canned varieties. If giving this food to your pet as a treat, make sure to feed it in moderation. Treats should make up less than 10% of your pet's daily caloric intake.

Tomatoes rank No. 27 on the Environmental Working Group's “Shopper’s Guide to Pesticides in Produce,” which ranks the most pesticide-ridden crops in the U.S.19 So as much as possible buy organic or "spray-free" tomatoes from local farmers markets, in order to minimize your pet's exposure to harmful pesticides and insecticides.

  • 4 Indian J Clin Biochem. 2013 Sep 1;28(4):314–328, Abstract

item.title: The Pet Longevity Marker Almost Everyone Ignores
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • During exercise, your dog’s body produces free radicals, which are DNA-damaging molecules that cause oxidative stress
  • It’s important to ensure all dogs, and especially canine athletes, are consuming adequate amounts of antioxidants to protect against free radical damage
  • A study of hunting dogs concludes that supplementing antioxidants can help them maintain healthy levels of important nutrients throughout hunting season
  • Fresh foods are the best way to provide antioxidants to your dog; it’s also important to ensure your canine companion is getting adequate dietary taurine to protect his heart — especially if he’s an athlete
  • Athletic dogs need a nutrient-dense diet that provides optimum energy in a small quantity of food; the protein source should be excellent-quality and animal-based, and the diet should be relatively high in dietary fat

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 3, 2018.

You may or may not know that during exercise, your dog's body (and yours) produces free radicals like crazy. It seems counterintuitive, because it doesn't make sense that exercise, which is good for the body, triggers the production of boatloads of DNA-damaging molecules as an end-byproduct.

But since that is indeed what occurs when bodies exercise, it's important to consider what type of diet is best for canine athletes, since they may need to consume more antioxidants than less active dogs to protect against free radical damage. Fortunately, the study sheds some light on the subject.

Researchers Measured Antioxidant Levels in American Foxhounds During Hunting Season

A team of university scientists and two pet food industry representatives conducted the study, which was published in the Journal of Animal Science.1 The dogs involved in the study were American Foxhound hunting dogs.

The researchers visited the dogs' kennel in Alabama during a single hunting season, and provided one group of with a "high-performance commercial diet," and another group with a similar diet supplemented with antioxidants, including vitamins C and E, lutein, zinc and taurine. During the course of the study, dogs from both groups were taken to hunt for two to five hours at a time, two to three times a week.

"We think of it as unstructured endurance exercise," says study author Kelly Swanson, Ph.D., a professor in the department of animal sciences and the division of nutritional sciences at the University of Illinois. "They're not running the entire time. They might stop to sniff or go more slowly to pick up a scent."2

The researchers took blood samples from the dogs to evaluate oxidative stress markers and other blood metabolites before they were put on the diets, and four additional times during the seven-month study.

Antioxidant-Supplemented Dogs Had Less Oxidative Stress and Stable Taurine and Vitamin E Levels

The researchers anticipated that the dogs eating the antioxidant-enriched diet would have lower levels of oxidative stress and improved performance compared to the other group. The study results showed the dogs did have improved measures of oxidative stress, but there didn't appear to be a difference in their level of performance compared to the other group.

"It turns out performance wasn't affected by diet," said Swanson, "but the test diet did improve indirect measures of oxidative stress. Therefore, improved performance may be expected with more strenuous exercise when metabolic demands are higher."

The researchers also discovered that over the course of the hunting season, the dogs fed the diet without antioxidant supplementation showed a decline in both taurine, an important nutrient for heart health, and vitamin E. One of the dogs even came close to a "critically low" level of taurine during the study.

Taurine and vitamin E levels for the dogs eating the supplemented diet remained at or above the baseline, which suggests these nutrients are compromised in athletic dogs over months of unstructured exercise. The researchers also believe more active dogs (e.g., sled dogs) may experience even greater nutrient depletion.

"We can conclude that athletic dogs may benefit from supplementation of vitamin E and taurine to minimize oxidation and maintain taurine status," Swanson says.

A Word About Taurine Levels in Dog Food

If you haven’t read this important article about taurine and heart disease in dogs, it’s worth doing so. A link has been established between grain-free dog food formulas and taurine deficiency in certain dogs that can lead to dilated cardiomyopathy, a heart muscle disease.

Until more information is available on the subject, the current recommendation is to supplement all dogs with high-taurine foods, no matter what type of diet they're eating. An easy way to do this is to simply mix a can of sardines into your pet's meal once a week. You can also find the taurine content of many other foods on page two of this study and also in this Raw Feeding Community article.

Fresh Foods Are the Best Source of Antioxidants for Dogs

As noted earlier, antioxidants are beneficial molecules that neutralize the toxic free radicals floating around in your pet's body before they can harm healthy cells and tissue, thereby reducing oxidative stress and DNA damage. As such, they play a key role in longevity, and high levels of circulating antioxidants are commonly seen in the "oldest old" among us.

Several studies of older dogs have proved the benefits of an antioxidant-rich diet for the aging canine brain.3,4,5,6 The results of a seven-year study of 90 cats aged 7 to 17 who were fed an antioxidant-rich diet showed fewer decreases in lean muscle mass; improved body weight, lean body mass, skin thickness and red cell quality; decreased incidence of disease; general improvement in quality of life; and significantly longer life span.7

The same is true for dogs. The more free radicals the body makes, the more antioxidants the body requires, and research shows puppies may have antioxidant deficiencies.

Most commercially available pet foods, even high-quality formulas, contain synthetic vitamins and minerals that have not undergone absorption or assimilation studies. Your dog's body is designed to absorb nutrients from fresh, living foods very efficiently. Antioxidants are contained in the vitamins in fresh foods, including:

  • Vitamin A and carotenoids, which are found in liver and bright-colored fruits and veggies like apricots, broccoli, cantaloupe, carrots, peaches, squash, sweet potatoes and tomatoes
  • Vitamin C, found in citrus fruits and strawberries, as well as green peppers, broccoli and green leafy vegetables
  • Vitamin E, found in nuts and seeds
  • Selenium, found in protein sources like nuts, fish, chicken, beef and eggs

Phytochemicals also contain antioxidant properties:

  • Flavonoids/polyphenols are in berries and tea (decaffeinated, for pets)
  • Lycopene is in tomatoes and watermelon
  • Lutein sources are dark green vegetables like spinach, broccoli and kale
  • Lignan is found in seeds

But since that is indeed what occurs when bodies exercise, it's important to consider what type of diet is best for canine athletes, since they may need to consume more antioxidants than less active dogs to protect against free radical damage. Researchers Measured Antioxidant Levels in American Foxhounds During Hunting Season

A team of university scientists and two pet food industry representatives conducted the study, which was published in the Journal of Animal Science.1 The dogs involved in the study were American Foxhound hunting dogs.

STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is not a single disease, but a group of chronic gastrointestinal changes driven by a buildup of inflammatory cells in the lining of the digestive tract
  • Common signs of IBD include chronic diarrhea, vomiting, blood or mucus in the stool, weight loss, reduced appetite, and low energy
  • Contributing factors include food sensitivity or intolerance, unbalanced gut (gut dysbiosis), parasitic infections, chronic stress, and environmental toxins
  • Management starts with calming the digestive tract with herbal therapy and restoring the normal flora, followed by a gradual transition to balanced, fresh food diet built around novel proteins
  • Long-term care should also look beyond food by limiting anything that may cause inflammation including reviewing vaccination schedules, avoiding a kibble-based diet, reviewing your pet’s medications, and reducing any environmental exposure that may contribute to ongoing inflammation

Digestive problems are among the most common reasons pet parents visit the veterinarian.1 Occasional vomiting or a bout of diarrhea usually resolves on its own, but when these episodes become chronic, the problem is often more than a passing stomach upset.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is one condition that may be behind ongoing gastrointestinal trouble in dogs and cats. It involves persistent inflammation within the digestive tract, which can gradually interfere with normal gut function.2 Understanding what may be driving the problem can help you and your veterinarian find an approach that better supports your pet's individual needs.

What Is IBD?

IBD is not a single disease but a collective term for a group of chronic gastrointestinal conditions driven by an abnormal buildup of inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, and sometimes neutrophils, in the lining of the digestive tract. These cells normally help defend the body against harmful substances, but with IBD they accumulate within the intestinal tissues and fuel persistent inflammation.3

Over time, that inflammation can change the structure of the digestive tract itself. The lining may become irritated, thickened, or ulcerated, and its integrity can deteriorate. Because this lining plays a significant role in digestion and nutrient absorption, ongoing damage can make it harder for your pet to absorb nutrients efficiently and lead to a deficiency (especially of vitamin B12 which is absorbed in the small intestine).4

The normal movement of food through the gastrointestinal tract may also be disrupted, with digestion speeding up in some animals and slowing down in others. Common signs of IBD include:5,6

  • Chronic or recurring diarrhea or loose stools
  • Vomiting or regurgitation
  • Mucus or fresh blood in the stool
  • Constipation or difficulty passing stool
  • Gas, bloating, or abdominal tenderness
  • Reduced appetite
  • Low energy
  • Weight loss

The pattern can differ from one pet to another. Because many gastrointestinal problems can cause similar signs, these symptoms alone do not confirm IBD. Persistent or recurring digestive trouble warrants veterinary evaluation to determine what is happening in your pet’s gut.7

What Causes IBD in Pets?

The exact cause of IBD is not fully understood, and in most cases, there is no single explanation. But several contributing factors show up consistently, and many of them are within a pet parent's ability to address. These include:8,9

  • Food sensitivities and intolerances — The dominant theory behind IBD is that the cells lining the GI tract can become hypersensitive to specific foods. Common triggers include wheat, corn, soy, dairy, chicken, and artificial flavorings or colorings.

    What makes food-related IBD particularly difficult to pin down is that reactions are often delayed. Most pets also eat the same food every day, and that repeated exposure to the same proteins and ingredients — beef and chicken being common examples — can increase the likelihood of an intolerance developing over time.
  • Gut dysbiosis — A healthy gut depends on a balanced population of bacteria. When the balance of these organisms shifts, a state known as dysbiosis can develop, which is intricately linked to increased intestinal permeability, loss of immune tolerance, and activation of inflammatory immune responses. This is sometimes caused by repeated courses of antibiotics, especially in pets with recurrent allergies.

    Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), in which bacteria proliferate in a part of the GI tract where they do not belong in high numbers, may also occur alongside digestive dysfunction and further disturb the intestinal environment.
  • Over-vaccination and chronic medications — Vaccines are manufactured using animal-derived cells, such as chicken embryo and bovine serum, to grow the antigen, and tiny amounts of those food proteins can remain in the final product. Because vaccines provoke a strong immune response, the immune system may learn to treat those residual proteins as threats and react when it encounters them again in food. Titers can be used to evaluate your pet’s current immunity, and a review of your pet’s lifestyle will help to see what their current disease exposure and risk is.

    Over-medication is also a concern. Long-term use of immunosuppressive drugs or repeated exposure to certain medications can compromise the immune system's ability to regulate itself, contributing to chronic, unresolved inflammation. A holistic vet can review your pet’s current medications and help your pet transition to a more natural lifestyle if indicated.
  • Stress — Chronic stress can trigger a sustained low-grade release of cortisol, which can slow digestion, impair gut motility, and activate mast cells in the GI tract — all of which feed directly into bowel inflammation. Stress is often overlooked as a contributor to IBD, but its effect on digestive function is well-established. Your pet may need treatment such as acupuncture or herbal remedies to help them deal with stress.
  • Environmental toxins — Toxins in your pet's environment or daily routine can also contribute to ongoing inflammation. These are worth auditing alongside diet and medication, particularly when IBD symptoms persist despite dietary changes. There is lab testing available to see if your pet has been exposed to harmful levels of environmental toxins and a detox may be necessary.

Getting the Right Diagnosis

A definitive IBD diagnosis has traditionally required an intestinal biopsy, a small tissue sample taken during an endoscopy procedure and sent to a pathology lab for analysis.10 While it is considered the confirmatory test, it is invasive, expensive, and requires anesthesia. A less invasive alternative is an abdominal ultrasound to visualize the internal organs and look for any thickening of the intestines or abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes or the presence of fluid.

Your vet may also recommend various blood tests for your pet. Bloodwork can show several conditions that may be related to gut health. These include testing vitamin B, Cobalamin, and Folate for intestinal malabsorption that can occur with IBD, as well as for SIBO or bacterial overgrowth. Other testing may include your pet’s protein and albumin levels for a condition called PLE or protein losing enteropathy that can cause thickened intestines due to protein loss.

Because secondary pancreatitis is common in IBD patients, testing pancreatic function is also worth discussing with your veterinarian. A CPL test can be done in the clinic and can quickly determine if your pet has pancreatitis. Other tests including PLI (Pancreatic Lipase Immunoreactivity) or PSL are also available to evaluate pancreatic function. Alternatively, if your vet is concerned that your pet’s pancreas may not be producing enough enzymes — a condition called EPI (exocrine pancreas insufficiency); a TLI test (Trypsin-Like Immunoreactivity) test may be ordered.11,12

Fecal testing is another key component of IBD. A study published in Nature Microbiology found that researchers could predict with over 90% accuracy which dogs had IBD and which were not based solely on the microbial species present in fecal samples.13 Microbiome testing will show the levels of healthy and harmful intestinal bacteria present in your pet’s gut. If their gut is imbalanced, custom probiotics (or in severe cases a fecal transplant) containing healthy normal flora may be needed to restore your pet’s intestinal biome. Additional fecal tests that may be performed include testing for any parasites such as giardia which can contribute to inflammation in IBD.

6 Ways to Help Calm Your Pet’s Gut

If your pet has been diagnosed with IBD, diet is one of the first areas to address. The goal is to help reduce irritation, give the digestive tract time to settle, and then gradually build a longer-term plan that supports the gut without introducing too many changes at once. Here’s how you can get started:14

  1. Start with a smarter bland diet — During an active flare-up, a temporary bland diet can help give the digestive tract a break. A good initial option is cooked, fat-free ground turkey with 100% canned pumpkin or cooked sweet potato. Turkey keeps the meal low in fat, while pumpkin or sweet potato provides a gentler source of fiber. Your holistic vet may also give you herbal remedies to help reduce gut inflammation or beneficial clay to absorb toxins.
  2. Transition to a novel, fresh food diet — Once symptoms begin to improve, the next step is moving to a balanced, preferably fresh food (not kibble based) diet built around novel proteins — proteins your pet has not been exposed to before. As IBD can be due to food sensitivity or intolerance, this can reduce continued exposure to ingredients that may be contributing to an unwanted immune response.
  3. Rebuild the gut with probiotics — Introduce beneficial microorganisms that can help replenish and support a healthier intestinal microbiome. Natural food sources of live cultures include plain, unsweetened yogurt and kefir, which may be suitable in small amounts for pets that tolerate dairy. Choose products with live active cultures and no added sugar or artificial sweeteners. In some cases, your holistic vet may recommend a custom probiotic for your pet.
  4. Feed beneficial bacteria with prebiotics — Prebiotics are nondigestible fibers that nourish the beneficial bacteria already living in your pet’s gut. Natural sources include inulin from chicory root. Because pets with IBD can respond differently to fiber, introduce prebiotic foods gradually and in tiny amounts to make sure your pet tolerate it. Always collaborate with your holistic veterinarian to determine the type and amount your pet tolerates best.
  5. Consider gut-soothing supplements — Certain herbs, amino acids, and digestive aids may help calm the digestive lining and support healing:15
    • Slippery elm — Contains mucilage, which forms a soothing, protective coating over the digestive lining and may help calm irritated tissue.
    • Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) — This demulcent herb may help enhance mucosal protection in the esophagus and digestive tract, creating a barrier that may support recovery of damaged tissue.
    • L-glutamine — An amino acid involved in maintaining the integrity of the intestinal lining. Animal and clinical studies have shown that glutamine deprivation leads to mucosal atrophy and ulceration, making supplementation particularly relevant for pets with IBD.16
    • Digestive enzymes — Digestive enzymes help break down food more efficiently, which can reduce the burden on an already compromised GI tract, especially when food intolerances are part of the picture. These are especially important for any pets diagnosed with pancreatitis.
  6. Add anti-inflammatory support and fill nutritional gaps — Omega-3 fatty acids, most commonly from krill oil, may help reduce inflammation in the digestive tract.17 It is also worth checking for nutritional deficiencies that may be compounding the problem — low levels of vitamin D, B12, zinc, and magnesium have all been associated with impaired digestive function.

Whether these supplements are introduced before, during, or after a dietary change depends on your pet's individual situation. A holistic or integrative veterinarian can help design a protocol specific to your pet rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

Keeping Your Pet’s Gut on Track

IBD is not something that resolves with a single change. Introduce dietary shifts and supplements one at a time so you can tell what is helping and what is not. A simple log of what your pet eats, any supplements given, and how their digestion responds day to day can make it easier to spot patterns and adjust course. Remember to read all ingredients on the product label to ensure your pet does not get anything that can cause inflammation; especially if they are on a novel protein diet.

It is also worth looking beyond diet. Discuss future vaccination schedules and vaccine titers with your holistic veterinarian, evaluate your pet’s current medications for any potential triggers, and audit your pet's environment for potential sources of chronic inflammation. These factors are easy to overlook but can quietly undermine progress made elsewhere.

Sources and References

  • 1 Golden Heart Veterinary Care, October 8, 2025
  • 2, 3, 5, 8 Dogs Naturally, December 11, 2021
  • 4, 6, 7, 9, 15 My Pet Nutritionist, April 6, 2020
  • 10 VCA Hospitals, Inflammatory Bowel Disease in Dogs
  • 11 dvm360, December 9, 2014
  • 12 dvm360, April 1, 2021
  • 13 UC San Diego, October 3, 2016
  • 14 Wag, Natural Treatments for Inflammatory Bowel Disease in Dogs
  • 16 J Epithel Biol Pharmacol. 2011 Aug 22;5(Suppl 1-M7):47–54
  • 17 Berwick Clyde Vet, Benefits of Omega-3 and Omega-6 for Pets

item.title: Don't Expect Your Pet to Weather This Choice of Pet Food Well
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The processed pet food industry wants you to believe “carbs are good” for dogs and cats and that its “scientific data” doesn’t support the notion that grain-free is better than grains
  • Missing entirely from this and all similar “scientific data” is the nutrition dogs and cats evolved to eat, also known as their ancestral diet, or the fact that as carnivores, they have no nutritional requirement for carbs
  • If you feed kibble, it’s important to find out how much carb content the food contains, as typically it will be many times the maximum recommended amount
  • There are many other reasons to avoid feeding kibble, including the dubious quality of raw ingredients, the potential for cancer-causing byproducts and the lack of moisture
  • The best diet for dogs and cats is nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate, and grain and carb-free

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 1, 2018.

There’s a blogger for a pet food industry journal who’s working hard at “debunking pet food myths and misconceptions.” His background includes spending “multiple years developing, formulating and launching dog and cat foods as a senior executive with leading pet food companies.” The guy is clearly as passionate about feeding processed pet food as others are about avoiding it.

He tends to write mildly outrageous headlines for his blog posts, such as this one: “Why grain-free pet food isn’t better and carbs are good.”1 In the article, he focuses on extruded kibble “since this category makes up most of the pet food products in the marketplace today.” Sadly, he’s right about that. Way too many dogs and cats are still eating a junk food diet every day of their lives.

The point of his article is to make the case that grain-free formulas aren’t free of starches or carbohydrates (which is true), and that dogs and cats digest all forms of extruded starch, including grains, similarly. Therefore, he concludes, “The scientific data does not support the notion that grain free is better than grains.”

Conveniently missing from this blog post and all pet food industry articles touting the virtues of kibble is any mention of the ancestral diet of dogs and cats, which should be (but certainly isn’t) the foundational “scientific data” that is used to formulate pet diets.

Your Pet's Ancestral Diet

First and foremost, when deciding what to feed your dog or cat, it's important to remember that your pet is a carnivore. His genetic makeup and internal workings remain essentially the same as his wild carnivorous ancestors.

The ancestral diet of a carnivore includes lots of variety and seasonal variability because certain prey is more available at certain times of the year. Wild dogs and cats thrive by consuming fresh, living whole foods. The food is moisture-dense because prey animals are about 70% water, plus it's high in animal protein and minerals, and moderate in fat.

There are no obese rabbits or other small prey animals in the wild, which is why dogs and cats do best with a diet that contains moderate to low amounts of high-quality animal fat and a very low percentage of carbohydrates. The only carbs wild cats consume are what is naturally found in the gastrointestinal (GI) tracts of their prey, plus the occasional nibble of grass which provides added fiber and enzymes.

Wild dogs (including wolves) are facultative or scavenging carnivores, so their diets are more varied than wild cats. Like cats, they catch, kill and consume whole prey, but unlike cats, they also eat carrion (dead animals). Wild dogs also eat poop, grass, berries and other plant matter. In fact, research shows that up to 30% of the stomach contents of wolves contain plant matter.

No, Carbs Are NOT Good Nutrition for Dogs and Cats, and It’s Irresponsible to Claim Otherwise

The notion that carbohydrates are a biologically correct source of energy for dogs, and especially cats, is nonsense. Fat is nature’s very best energy source for carnivores, who actually have no carbohydrate requirement.

Contrary to what the pet food industry wants pet parents to believe, carbohydrates are not a “main macronutrient” required by dogs and cats. Neither the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) nor the European Pet Food Industry Federation (FEDIAF) stipulates a requirement for carbohydrates in pet food, because again, dogs and cats have no nutritional requirement for carbohydrates.

The fact is, calories from starchy carbohydrates should be less than 10% of the total calories consumed by your pet each day. The carb content of processed pet food, especially grain-free formulas, is typically many times the amount pets require.

The starch in these foods is converted to sugar. One of the biggest reasons behind the current epidemic of metabolic and inflammatory diseases in pets is likely the unnaturally high amounts of starch (sugar) in the processed pet foods fed to them over the last 50 years.

How to Determine the Carb Content of Kibble

To determine what percentage of the food you’re feeding your dog or cat is made up of carbohydrates, find the “guaranteed analysis” on the bag and apply the following formula:

100% - % protein - % fat - % moisture - % ash (if not listed, use 6%) = % carbs

Fiber is indigestible roughage that doesn't break down into sugar, so you don't have to include it in the formula.

Example, cat food: Royal Canin Indoor Adult Dry Cat Food

100% – 27% protein – 15% fat – 8% moisture – 6% ash = 44% carbs

Example, dog food: Royal Canin Medium Adult Dry Dog Food

100% – 23% protein – 12% fat – 10% moisture – 6% ash = 49% carbs

In both these examples, the amount of carbohydrates far exceeds the amount a cat or dog is able to effectively digest and assimilate. And believe it or not, most grain-free dry formulas are even higher in carbs than regular formulas like the Royal Canin products.

If you're feeding a dry diet, it might be free of grains, but it can't be free of carbs, because carbs are necessary to form kibble. If you look at the package label, you'll see potato, sweet potato, lentils, peas (pea starch), chickpeas, tapioca or another carbohydrate source(s).

Carb-heavy pet food can lead to blood sugar fluctuations, insulin resistance, obesity, diabetes and other health problems in pets. Carb intake above your dog’s or cat’s daily needs triggers internal enzyme factors to store the excess as body fat.

Carbs Aren’t the Only Problem with Kibble

While most kibble is formulated to meet the basic nutritional requirements of dogs and cats, it certainly doesn’t provide optimal nourishment for the long haul. Dry pet food raises several concerns, starting with the quality of the raw ingredients.

Rendering plants create meat and bone meal from a variety of dubious sources, for example, parts of cows that can't be sold for human consumption, including bones, the digestive system, the brain, udders, hide and more. The vast majority of pet foods are made with ingredients rejected by the human food industry, meaning they’re feed-grade.

They also may use the carcasses of diseased animals, expired grocery store meat (including the plastic and Styrofoam packaging), road kill, zoo animals and dogs and cats that have been euthanized. Here’s a stomach-turning description of the process of spinning these raw ingredients into pet food from Slate:

"This material is slowly pulverized into one big blend of dead stuff and meat packaging. It is then transferred into a vat where it is heated for hours to between 220 [to] 270 degrees F. At such high temperatures, the fat and grease float to the top along with any fat-soluble compounds or solids that get mixed up with them.
Most viruses and bacteria are killed. The fat can then be skimmed off, packaged and renamed. Most of this material is called 'meat and bone meal.' It can be used in livestock feed, pet food or fertilizer … There is essentially no federal enforcement of standards for the contents of pet food.
… Indeed, the same system that doesn't know whether its main ingredient is chicken beaks or Dachshund really cannot guarantee adequate nutrition to the dogs that eat it."2

The majority of dry pet food is a blend of poor-quality meats, byproducts and synthetic vitamins and minerals. In addition, most kibble contains high-glycemic, genetically engineered (GE) corn, wheat, rice or potato — grains and starches that have no place in a carnivore’s diet and create metabolically stressful insulin, glucagon and cortisol spikes throughout the day.

In the last 50 years, we've learned the hard way that feeding nutritionally unbalanced, biologically inappropriate diets to pets does not create health. In fact, chronic inflammatory and degenerative diseases in dogs and cats are at epidemic levels, and the problem can be traced directly to diet and lifestyle.

To make matters worse, the poor-quality proteins and fats used in most kibble, when processed at high temperatures, create cancerous byproducts such as heterocyclic amines. The meat that goes into dry pet food is put through at least four high-temperature cooking processes, leaving the digestibility, absorbability and overall nutrient value highly questionable.

The low moisture content of dry food is also problematic, especially for cats. Dry cat food provides only about one-tenth the amount of moisture cats receive from prey animals, living foods and even commercial canned diets, which puts significant stress on their kidneys and bladder. Dogs also tend to become excessively thirsty when fed a dry diet.

Feed Your Pet a Grain- and Starch-Free Species-Appropriate Diet

Feeding a species-appropriate diet means the food you offer your pet:

  • Is grain-free and carb-free — no corn, no wheat, no rice, no millet, no oatmeal, no potato, no sweet potato, no tapioca, no peas, etc.
  • Is in its biologically correct form — raw, whole, unadulterated and undenatured meat
  • Contains all the moisture needed for your pet's body to process the food with very little metabolic stress

The top recommendation is to feed a raw-food diet. It's grain-free, moisture-rich, living, and of course, fresh. An alternative recommendation is canned food or a gently dehydrated (air-dried) raw food that can be reconstituted with water to contain at least 70% moisture.

The difference between air dehydrated foods and extruded foods is temperature. Foods that aren’t cooked or extruded at high temperatures retain more nutritional value. When air-dried foods are reconstituted with water, they also become moisture-rich and significantly healthier than any dry kibble on the market.

Also check with the pet food manufacturer to make sure whatever food you choose is nutritionally balanced. Many of the new niche pet foods appearing on store shelves are intended for intermittent feeding only — it should say that on the label. This means the formula doesn't meet AAFCO standards for a complete and balanced pet food, and needs to be fed in rotation with other nutritionally complete foods to create a balanced diet for your furry companion.

Sources and References

  • 1 PetfoodIndustry.com, August 14, 2017
  • 2 Slate, April 19, 2013

item.title: Getting Lost Is Scary Getting Home Shouldn't Be
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • It’s important for pet guardians to insure all furry family members have current, legible ID tags or some other form of identification to help them find their way home in the event they are lost
  • Microchipping is an increasingly popular permanent method of identifying animals, and many dogs and cats adopted from shelters and rescues, as well as purebreds purchased from breeders, come to their new family already chipped
  • For those considering microchipping, there are pros and cons to consider. It’s up to each pet guardian to weigh the benefits against the risks and make an informed decision based on your pet’s individual personality and lifestyle
  • Another way to permanently ID your pet is a tattoo. This method, too, has pros and cons depending on your individual situation, and it’s important to make an informed decision for your pet
  • A microchip is only useful if it’s registered and the contact information in the recovery database is kept up to date

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 20, 2015.

It’s important to insure your dog, cat or other companion animal is equipped with up-to-date ID information in the event he gets separated from you. Sadly, the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) found that while 80% of pet owners realize the importance of ID tags, just 33% say their pet always wears one.1

If you’re among the majority of pet guardians who aren’t always as disciplined as you would like to be about ID tags, the good news is that tags aren’t the only way to identify your pet in the event she is lost. There are actually several other methods for identifying dogs and cats, including GPS tracking devices, radio frequency identification devices, microchips, and tattoos. The most popular method for ID’ing pets, second only to ID tags, is microchipping.

How Microchipping Works

The pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice. It is injected under the skin in the neck area between the shoulders, and provides a permanent means of identifying your pet.

Microchip placement is very similar to a vaccination. A bit of loose skin between the animal’s shoulder blades is gently pulled up, and the needle containing the chip is inserted. The trigger is depressed, injecting the microchip beneath the skin.

Each chip is equipped with an electromagnetic transponder with a unique code that needs to be registered with a recovery program like HomeAgain or Avid. Before it is placed, the chip is scanned while still in the package to validate that the identification code of the transponder matches the code printed on the package label. Once inserted in your pet, it is scanned again to verify that it can be read.

If a pet is lost, most veterinary offices, shelters, and humane societies have scanners that can locate the chip inside the animal’s body and read the code on it. So as long as your pet’s microchip has been registered and your information is up-to-date in the recovery program database, the vet clinic or shelter should be able to reunite you with your furry family member.

Pros and Cons of Microchipping

Microchips have become extremely popular. Many shelters now implant chips in every animal before he or she goes home with a new family. And chips have become a standard method of identifying strays. Any lost animal brought to a veterinary clinic or animal shelter is automatically scanned for at least the two most common brands (HomeAgain and Avid). The primary benefit of microchipping is, of course, that your pet can’t lose his ID.

One drawback is that the insertion of the chip can be a bit painful like any injection. A local anesthetic can be used when inserting a microchip to alleviate any discomfort.

Another potential disadvantage is that chips have been known to migrate away from the injection site, which makes them more difficult to locate with a scanner. Also, there are several microchip manufacturers, but to my knowledge, there’s no universal scanner that reads every brand of chip.

Another extremely important point to remember about microchips is that your pet’s chip should be registered to be of any use, and your contact information needs to be kept up to date in the recovery program database for the same reason.

Also, the people doing the scanning should know how to correctly and thoroughly scan a pet to locate a microchip — especially one that may have migrated away from the injection site.

Health Concerns Related to Microchips

The primary concern any time something foreign is introduced into the body — whether it’s a microchip or, say, a metal plate to repair a fractured bone, or a transplanted organ — is the potential for the body to reject the foreign material.

There have been documented cases in veterinary medicine of sarcomas or fibrosarcomas (soft tissue tumors) developing at microchip injection sites. Research shows that between 1996 and 2006, between 0.8% and 10.2% of laboratory animals developed malignant tumors around or near implanted microchips. There are also two documented cases of chip-related malignancies in dogs.2

The recommended approach, if you’re considering chipping your pet, is to assess how much risk there is that she will ever get out of your sight. If you have an indoor-only cat, for example, or a well-trained (responsive) dog that is always on a leash outdoors, the potential risks of microchipping are often considered to outweigh the benefits.

An Alternative to Microchipping: A Permanent Tattoo

This method of ID’ing your pet involves tattooing a unique code or information on the inner pinna (ear flap), the tummy or inner leg of a mature (fully grown) pet. Ideally, ID tattoos are done while an animal is under anesthesia for another procedure. Otherwise, a sedative and local anesthesia should be used.

Tattooing is a method commonly used to permanently identify pets. A phone number that rarely changes can be placed on the inner thighs. Obviously, if your phone number or other personal information changes frequently, this may not be a good option for you.

Another potential downside is that you have to hope the person who finds your pet knows to look for a tattoo, and this is especially challenging if your pet is very furry. In this case, the earflap is a better location for a tattoo, but many people don’t like earflap markings for aesthetic reasons.

You can increase the likelihood of your tattooed pet being returned by registering the number with AKC Reunite, the National Dog Registry, or Tattoo-a-Pet. Any number can be registered with the National Dog Registry, and all tattooed animals can be enrolled in AKC Reunite program regardless of species, age, size or number used.

A drawback to a tattoo is that it may fade or blur over time and become difficult to read. Another layer of black ink can be applied to restore the tattoo.

Each method for ID'ing your pet has pros and cons, so the ultimate decision is yours and should be based on your pet's personality and lifestyle, as well as your comfort level with the identification method you choose for your furry family member.

It’s recommended that every pet have a standard up-to-date ID collar or tag in addition to whatever other ID method their owner chooses, since the easiest, fastest way for someone who has found your pet to find you, is to take a quick look at the contact info contained on his tag or collar.

Sources and References

  • Webvet
  • 1 ASPCA.org
  • 2 AntiChips.com
